column1: What is a 'collision domain' and how does a hub vs. a bridge affect it?
column2: A collision domain is a network segment where simultaneous transmissions can collide. A hub extends a single collision domain across all ports (Layer 1 repeater); a bridge/switch creates a separate collision domain per port since it forwards selectively instead of blindly repeating.

column1: How does a bridge/switch build its MAC address table, and what happens when the destination MAC is unknown?
column2: It records the source MAC address and ingress port of every frame it sees. If the destination MAC is unknown, it floods the frame out every port except the one it arrived on.

column1: What catastrophic failure mode occurs when a Layer 2 network contains a physical loop without STP?
column2: A broadcast storm: frames circulate endlessly, duplicating at every switch port, saturating bandwidth within seconds and causing exponential MAC address table thrashing as switches see the same source MAC from multiple ports.

column1: Why can't Ethernet natively handle loops the way Layer 3 routing can?
column2: Ethernet frames carry no hop count/TTL field and switches forward purely on destination MAC lookups with no global topology awareness, unlike IP where TTL provides intrinsic loop protection.

column1: What are the three cascading elections performed by the Spanning Tree Protocol?
column2: 1) Elect a single root bridge (lowest bridge ID). 2) Each non-root switch elects its root port (best path to root). 3) Each segment elects a designated bridge/port to forward traffic; all other ports on that segment go into blocking state.

column1: What is the central invariant that TCAM-based hardware forwarding provides in multilayer switches?
column2: Constant-time forwarding regardless of table size — forwarding latency becomes a hardware property (bounded by silicon signal propagation) independent of control plane state size.

column1: How does CAM/TCAM lookup differ fundamentally from conventional RAM access?
column2: In RAM, the CPU supplies an address and gets data back. In CAM/TCAM, the switch supplies data (a MAC address or IP prefix) and the memory returns the matching address — the lookup operation is inverted, enabling single-clock-cycle parallel lookups.

column1: What ternary logic feature does TCAM add over standard CAM, and what does it enable?
column2: Each bit position can be 0, 1, or 'don't care,' enabling wildcard/longest-prefix-match routing lookups without iterative tree traversal.

column1: What is the architectural distinction between a switch's control plane and data plane?
column2: The control plane (software on the management CPU) handles the slow path of route/MAC learning and protocol state machines (STP, routing); the data plane (hardware ASIC) handles the fast path of per-packet forwarding at line rate.

column1: What problem does Link Aggregation (LAG) solve, and what constraint must switch ASICs honor when distributing frames across member links?
column2: LAG combines multiple physical links into one logical channel, providing both increased bandwidth and graceful degradation on link failure. ASICs must distribute frames across member links without reordering packets within the same flow.

column1: Why does QoS prioritization exist on switch egress ports specifically, rather than being solved by adding bandwidth?
column2: An egress port is a strict serialization bottleneck — only one frame can transmit at any instant. When ingress traffic exceeds egress capacity, frames queue and can tail-drop; QoS classification and scheduling let time-sensitive flows (e.g., VoIP) preempt bulk traffic for transmission slots.

column1: What vulnerability does unrestricted MAC learning on access ports create, and what feature mitigates it?
column2: Unrestricted learning allows any source MAC observed on a port to populate the forwarding table, enabling trivial MAC spoofing attacks. Port security mitigates this by restricting which/how many MAC addresses are allowed to be learned on a given port.
